ACTC1.relevance: Cardiac alpha-actin forms the thin filament. Disease-associated variants can alter force generation and produce hypertrophic, dilated, or noncompaction phenotypes.
ACTC1.consideration: Interpret against the specific cardiomyopathy phenotype and family segregation.

ACTN2.relevance: Alpha-actinin-2 anchors the sarcomere at the Z-disc. Pathogenic variants cause a spectrum of cardiac disease, sometimes with skeletal muscle involvement.
ACTN2.consideration: A core addition in the PDF; the 2025 HCM reappraisal supports definitive disease validity.

ALPK3.relevance: ALPK3 supports cardiomyocyte structure. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants can cause HCM; biallelic disease often presents earlier and more severely.
ALPK3.consideration: Confirm zygosity and mechanism. The HCM reappraisal distinguishes strong dominant from definitive recessive evidence.

BAG3.relevance: BAG3 helps maintain protein quality in cardiac muscle. Loss-of-function variants are associated with dilated cardiomyopathy; certain variants produce severe multisystem myopathy.
BAG3.consideration: Consider skeletal weakness, neuropathy, and variant-specific syndromic presentations.

CAV3.relevance: Caveolin-3 organizes muscle membrane caveolae. It is retained in both source panels, but its skeletal muscle disease association must be separated from proposed cardiac associations.
CAV3.consideration: Do not infer a monogenic arrhythmia diagnosis from panel inclusion. Review the exact gene-disease pair.
CAV3.caution: Congenital LQTS evidence is limited or disputed; isolated cardiomyopathy claims also require careful review.

CRYAB.relevance: Alpha-B crystallin protects structural proteins under stress. Some disease-associated variants produce myofibrillar muscle disease with cardiac involvement.
CRYAB.consideration: Ask about cataracts and skeletal weakness; isolated HCM evidence should be reviewed separately.
CRYAB.caution: Retained broad-panel gene; evidence depends on the syndrome and variant mechanism.

CSRP3.relevance: Muscle LIM protein participates in sarcomere organization and stress sensing. CSRP3-related HCM can show a dosage effect, with more severe disease in biallelic individuals.
CSRP3.consideration: The 2025 reappraisal supports definitive semidominant HCM; consider allele dosage and segregation.

DES.relevance: Desmin connects the muscle contractile apparatus to the cell scaffold. Desminopathy may combine cardiomyopathy, atrioventricular block, arrhythmia, and skeletal muscle weakness.
DES.consideration: Conduction disease can be prominent. Review rhythm findings alongside imaging and neuromuscular assessment.

DMD.relevance: Dystrophin stabilizes the muscle cell membrane. Dystrophinopathy may cause dilated cardiomyopathy before, or with little, skeletal muscle disease; heterozygous females may be affected.
DMD.consideration: Require validated exon deletion/duplication analysis as well as sequencing. Assess cardiac risk in female relatives.

DSC2.relevance: Desmocollin-2 is a desmosomal adhesion protein. Pathogenic variants can weaken mechanical coupling and cause arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with right, left, or biventricular involvement.
DSC2.consideration: Interpret with ACM criteria, imaging, rhythm phenotype, and family segregation.

DSG2.relevance: Desmoglein-2 links neighboring cardiac cells through desmosomes. Disease-associated variants can produce ventricular arrhythmia and progressive myocardial dysfunction.
DSG2.consideration: Electrical disease may precede obvious ventricular dysfunction; assess both structural and rhythm features.

DSP.relevance: Desmoplakin anchors desmosomes to the cytoskeleton. DSP cardiomyopathy often affects the left ventricle and may present with myocardial injury episodes, fibrosis, and ventricular arrhythmia.
DSP.consideration: Review CMR fibrosis and myocarditis-like episodes. Woolly hair or palmoplantar keratoderma suggests a cardiocutaneous phenotype.

FHL1.relevance: FHL1 participates in muscle structure and signaling. Its disorders may combine hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with weakness, muscle hypertrophy, or contractures.
FHL1.consideration: A neuromuscular examination and X-linked pedigree can clarify an apparently isolated cardiac presentation.

FHOD3.relevance: FHOD3 regulates actin organization in cardiomyocytes. Pathogenic variants can disrupt sarcomere maintenance and cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
FHOD3.consideration: New in the PDF; the 2025 ClinGen HCM reappraisal supports definitive validity. Check variant mechanism and segregation.

FLNC.relevance: Filamin-C links and stabilizes the muscle cytoskeleton. Truncating variants are associated with arrhythmogenic dilated disease, whereas some missense variants cause hypertrophic or myopathic phenotypes.
FLNC.consideration: Mechanism matters: do not transfer a truncating-variant risk profile to every FLNC variant.

GLA.phenotypes: Fabry disease;LVH / HCM mimic;Renal disease;Neuropathic pain
GLA.relevance: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease, a potentially treatable storage disorder that can mimic sarcomeric HCM. Late cardiac-predominant disease may lack classic systemic signs.
GLA.consideration: Correlate the variant with biochemical testing. Normal enzyme activity does not exclude disease in females; confirmed disease merits specialist therapy assessment.

JPH2.relevance: Junctophilin-2 maintains the junction between the cell membrane and sarcoplasmic reticulum, enabling coordinated calcium release during contraction.
JPH2.consideration: Evaluate inheritance and phenotype carefully; dominant HCM and recessive early-onset disease require different interpretation.
JPH2.caution: HCM evidence is moderate in the 2025 reappraisal; review the exact variant and disease pair.

JUP.relevance: Plakoglobin is a desmosomal component. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause Naxos disease, combining arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma.
JUP.consideration: Examine skin and hair and establish zygosity; monoallelic findings need phenotype-specific review.

LMNA.relevance: Lamin A/C supports the nuclear envelope. LMNA-related cardiomyopathy often begins with conduction disease or arrhythmia before substantial left ventricular dilation or systolic impairment.
LMNA.consideration: A confirmed pathogenic variant can inform specialist arrhythmic risk assessment and family surveillance. Consider neuromuscular features and a three-generation pedigree.

MYBPC3.relevance: Cardiac myosin-binding protein C regulates sarcomere contraction. Loss-of-function variants are a major cause of inherited HCM with age-dependent and variable expression.
MYBPC3.consideration: A normal assessment in a young relative does not exclude later expression. Consider biallelic disease in severe infantile presentations.

MYH7.relevance: Beta-myosin heavy chain drives muscle contraction. Specific pathogenic variants produce different cardiac and skeletal muscle phenotypes.
MYH7.consideration: Variant location and mechanism are important; a truncating variant is not automatically a typical MYH7-HCM allele.

MYL2.relevance: Myosin regulatory light chain modulates sarcomere contraction. Dominant pathogenic variants can cause HCM; recessive disease can have severe early cardiac and skeletal involvement.
MYL2.consideration: Match zygosity and variant class to the phenotype, particularly in infants.

MYL3.relevance: Myosin essential light chain contributes to force generation. Disease-associated variants can produce hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, including biallelic presentations.
MYL3.consideration: Review allele dosage, segregation, and the specific variant evidence.

NEXN.relevance: Nexilin supports cardiac membrane and cytoskeletal organization. Rare NEXN variants have been associated with dilated cardiomyopathy, including severe biallelic presentations.
NEXN.consideration: The 2026 DCM reassessment upgraded the evidence. The PDF’s second-priority inclusion label is historical; assess current inheritance- and variant-specific evidence.
NEXN.caution: HCM evidence remains limited in the 2025 reappraisal. A DCM association must not be transferred to an HCM interpretation.

PKP2.relevance: Plakophilin-2 helps assemble cardiac desmosomes. Pathogenic variants are an important cause of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and related electrical disease.
PKP2.consideration: Assess imaging, rhythm phenotype, and family history together; penetrance is variable and age-dependent.

PLN.relevance: Phospholamban regulates calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Certain pathogenic variants cause dilated or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.
PLN.consideration: Risk differs by variant. Avoid applying founder-variant outcome data to all PLN changes.

PRKAG2.relevance: The AMPK gamma-2 subunit regulates cellular energy sensing. PRKAG2 syndrome causes cardiac glycogen accumulation that can mimic HCM, often with pre-excitation and later conduction disease.
PRKAG2.consideration: LVH plus a short PR interval or pre-excitation should prompt review for this HCM phenocopy.

PTPN11.phenotypes: Noonan spectrum;Pulmonary stenosis;HCM in selected syndromes
PTPN11.relevance: SHP2 regulates RAS-MAPK signaling. PTPN11 variants cause RASopathies, with cardiac findings that differ between Noonan syndrome and Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines.
PTPN11.consideration: Assess dysmorphism, growth, lentigines, and congenital heart disease; syndrome-specific variant effects matter.

RAF1.relevance: RAF1 is part of RAS-MAPK signaling. Certain activating variants cause Noonan-spectrum disease with a substantial association with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
RAF1.consideration: Consider syndromic assessment even when HCM dominates the presentation.

RBM20.relevance: RBM20 controls splicing of cardiac proteins, including titin. Pathogenic variants can cause dilated cardiomyopathy with prominent arrhythmic disease.
RBM20.consideration: Variant location and functional mechanism matter; isolated HCM claims should be reviewed separately.

RIT1.relevance: RIT1 regulates cellular signaling. Activating pathogenic variants cause a Noonan-spectrum disorder in which hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may be an early feature.
RIT1.consideration: Review growth, facial features, congenital heart defects, and perinatal history.

RYR2.relevance: The cardiac ryanodine receptor releases stored calcium for contraction. Gain-of-function variants typically cause CPVT; other mechanisms can cause distinct arrhythmic phenotypes.
RYR2.consideration: Exercise or emotion-triggered syncope is a key clue. Source-panel overlap does not mean every RYR2 variant causes structural cardiomyopathy.
RYR2.caution: Cardiac phenotype depends on mechanism; structural cardiomyopathy claims need separate evidence.

SCN5A.relevance: Nav1.5 carries the cardiac sodium current. Gain- and loss-of-function variants can produce different phenotypes, including long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, conduction disease, and some dilated cardiomyopathy.
SCN5A.consideration: Interpret the specific variant mechanism with the ECG and clinical context. Opposing channel effects cannot be assumed from the gene name.

SGCD.relevance: Delta-sarcoglycan stabilizes the muscle membrane. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause a muscular dystrophy that can involve the heart.
SGCD.consideration: Look for muscle weakness and elevated CK. An isolated heterozygous finding needs cautious interpretation.
SGCD.caution: Established recessive muscle disease should not be conflated with a definitive dominant isolated DCM association.

TCAP.relevance: Telethonin contributes to sarcomere Z-disc assembly. Biallelic disease is associated with muscular dystrophy; proposed isolated cardiomyopathy associations have weaker support.
TCAP.consideration: Review neuromuscular findings, zygosity, and the current gene-disease curation.
TCAP.caution: Isolated dominant HCM association is disputed in the 2025 reappraisal.

TNNC1.relevance: Cardiac troponin C binds calcium to regulate contraction. Variant-specific changes in calcium sensitivity can cause hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy.
TNNC1.consideration: The 2025 HCM reappraisal upgraded TNNC1 to definitive HCM validity.

TNNI3.relevance: Cardiac troponin I inhibits actin-myosin interaction until calcium activation. Pathogenic variants can cause hypertrophic, restrictive, or dilated phenotypes.
TNNI3.consideration: Restrictive physiology with relatively little hypertrophy can be a useful clue; assess variant and inheritance.

TNNT2.relevance: Cardiac troponin T links the troponin complex to tropomyosin. Disease-associated variants affect calcium-regulated contraction and can produce multiple cardiomyopathy phenotypes.
TNNT2.consideration: Do not estimate sudden-death risk from the gene alone; integrate personal and family clinical findings.

TPM1.relevance: Alpha-tropomyosin regulates access of myosin to actin. Variant-specific effects on thin-filament regulation can cause hypertrophic or dilated disease.
TPM1.consideration: Use the observed cardiac phenotype, variant mechanism, and segregation to guide interpretation.

TTN.relevance: Titin provides sarcomere elasticity and structural support. Truncating variants in relevant cardiac-expressed exons are an important cause of dilated cardiomyopathy.
TTN.consideration: Exon usage, transcript, location, and variant class matter. Many rare missense variants remain uncertain.
TTN.caution: Presence in the arrhythmia panel does not establish a primary channelopathy association.

TTR.relevance: Transthyretin can form amyloid deposits in the heart and nerves. Hereditary ATTR amyloidosis is an important cause of increased ventricular wall thickness that can resemble HCM.
TTR.consideration: Distinguish variant from wild-type ATTR; coordinate amyloid evaluation and exclude light-chain disease as clinically indicated.

VCL.relevance: Vinculin links cell adhesion complexes to the actin cytoskeleton. Selected pathogenic variants have been associated with dilated cardiomyopathy.
VCL.consideration: Interpret with segregation, phenotype, and current evidence; penetrance may be reduced.
VCL.caution: Review current gene-disease validity and variant mechanism; not all rare VCL variants are causal.

CACNA1C.relevance: Cav1.2 carries L-type calcium current. Variant-specific dysfunction can cause long QT and Timothy-spectrum disease, sometimes with syndactyly or neurodevelopmental features.
CACNA1C.consideration: Distinguish syndromic CACNA1C disease from isolated LQTS; phenotype and mechanism change the interpretation.
CACNA1C.caution: Evidence for isolated LQTS differs from definitive syndromic disease; Brugada claims require separate review.

CACNB2.relevance: The calcium-channel beta-2 subunit regulates channel function. The PDF retains CACNB2 as a historical arrhythmia-panel gene, but biological plausibility is not proof of causation.
CACNB2.consideration: Prioritize validated disease genes and review expert curation before using a result clinically.
CACNB2.caution: The ClinGen Brugada reappraisal classified non-SCN5A candidate genes, including CACNB2, as disputed.

CALM1.relevance: Calmodulin senses calcium and controls cardiac ion channels. Pathogenic CALM1 variants can cause severe early-onset repolarization or calcium-triggered arrhythmia disorders.
CALM1.consideration: Consider early presentation, marked QT prolongation, or exertional arrhythmia; evaluate variant-specific evidence.

CALM2.relevance: CALM2 encodes calmodulin, a calcium sensor essential for cardiac channel regulation. Pathogenic variants can cause severe childhood arrhythmia phenotypes.
CALM2.consideration: A negative family history does not exclude a de novo calmodulinopathy.

CALM3.relevance: CALM3 produces the same calmodulin protein as CALM1 and CALM2. Disruptive variants can impair channel regulation and cause severe early-onset arrhythmias.
CALM3.consideration: Interpret the specific variant and clinical phenotype; the gene name alone does not establish severity.

CASQ2.relevance: Calsequestrin-2 stores calcium inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Dysfunction can trigger adrenergically mediated ventricular arrhythmias, often with a normal resting ECG.
CASQ2.consideration: Biallelic disease is typical, but selected heterozygous variants can be relevant; assess zygosity and exercise phenotype.

GPD1L.relevance: GPD1L has been studied for effects on cardiac sodium-channel availability. It remains in the source list despite disputed evidence for monogenic Brugada causation.
GPD1L.consideration: Do not treat a rare GPD1L variant as a molecular diagnosis of Brugada syndrome.
GPD1L.caution: Brugada gene-disease validity is disputed; panel retention is historical context.

HCN4.phenotypes: Sinus bradycardia;Familial AF / tachycardia–bradycardia;LV noncompaction;Aortic dilation in some families
HCN4.relevance: HCN4 carries a pacemaker current in the sinus node. Selected variants have been described in families with sinus-node dysfunction, tachycardia–bradycardia and atrial fibrillation. Some HCN4 families also have structural cardiac features.
HCN4.consideration: Review resting rate, chronotropic response, atrial arrhythmias, imaging and family segregation. Interpret the specific variant and family phenotype; AF-focus placement does not exclude ventricular risk.

KCNE1.relevance: KCNE1 modulates the IKs potassium current. Biallelic pathogenic variants can cause long QT with congenital deafness; some alleles influence acquired QT susceptibility.
KCNE1.consideration: Separate biallelic syndromic disease from isolated dominant LQTS and medication-related susceptibility.
KCNE1.caution: Monoallelic isolated congenital LQTS has limited evidence; a risk allele is not equivalent to a monogenic diagnosis.

KCNE2.phenotypes: Acquired QT susceptibility;Historical congenital LQTS candidate
KCNE2.relevance: KCNE2 modulates potassium-channel function. Certain alleles may influence susceptibility to acquired QT prolongation, but monogenic congenital LQTS causation is disputed.
KCNE2.consideration: Interpret drug and electrolyte context and the exact allele; avoid a congenital LQTS diagnosis based solely on this gene.
KCNE2.caution: Congenital LQTS validity is disputed; susceptibility evidence addresses a different clinical question.

KCNH2.relevance: Kv11.1 carries the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current. Reduced current causes LQT2; different functional effects can cause other repolarization phenotypes.
KCNH2.consideration: Review QTc, T-wave morphology, medication exposure, electrolytes, and variant mechanism.

KCNJ2.relevance: Kir2.1 contributes to the inward rectifier potassium current. Pathogenic variants can cause Andersen-Tawil syndrome with ventricular arrhythmia, periodic paralysis, and characteristic physical features.
KCNJ2.consideration: Prominent U waves and bidirectional VT may be clues; distinguish the syndrome from isolated LQTS or typical CPVT.
KCNJ2.caution: Definitive syndromic disease is distinct from limited evidence for isolated congenital LQTS.

KCNQ1.relevance: Kv7.1 carries the slow delayed rectifier potassium current. Loss-of-function variants cause LQT1; biallelic variants can cause long QT with congenital sensorineural deafness.
KCNQ1.consideration: Consider exercise or swimming-triggered events, hearing status, zygosity, and the specific channel effect.

TECRL.relevance: TECRL-related disease disrupts cardiac calcium handling and can cause exercise- or emotion-triggered ventricular arrhythmias, sometimes with QT prolongation.
TECRL.consideration: Confirm two pathogenic alleles in trans where relevant. An isolated heterozygous finding does not establish recessive CPVT.

TMEM43.relevance: TMEM43 is associated with arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, particularly for well-characterized variants such as p.Ser358Leu.
TMEM43.consideration: Evidence and risk can be highly variant-specific; do not generalize founder-variant outcomes to every rare change.

TRDN.relevance: Triadin organizes calcium-release complexes in the heart. Biallelic loss-of-function variants can cause severe childhood ventricular arrhythmias, sometimes with QT prolongation.
TRDN.consideration: Confirm zygosity and phase. A single recessive allele generally requires further evaluation rather than a definitive diagnosis.

ACTA2.relevance: Smooth muscle alpha-actin supports arterial contraction. Pathogenic variants can cause heritable thoracic aneurysm and dissection, with extra-aortic vascular features in some individuals.
ACTA2.consideration: Review the entire vascular phenotype and family history; surveillance and intervention decisions require gene- and patient-specific assessment.

COL3A1.relevance: Type III collagen maintains vessel and hollow-organ integrity. Pathogenic variants cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with arterial and organ fragility.
COL3A1.consideration: Consider easy bruising, translucent skin, and personal or family arterial/organ rupture; obtain specialist assessment.

COL5A1.relevance: Type V collagen regulates collagen fibril assembly. Pathogenic variants typically cause classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, characterized by skin and joint findings.
COL5A1.consideration: Assess skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scars, and hypermobility; use syndrome-specific vascular interpretation.
COL5A1.caution: Classical EDS is not equivalent to definitive isolated HTAD; retained broad aortopathy-panel coverage.

COL5A2.relevance: The alpha-2 chain of type V collagen contributes to connective tissue integrity. Pathogenic variants can cause classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
COL5A2.consideration: Connect the result to skin, scar, and joint findings; evaluate the actual vascular phenotype separately.
COL5A2.caution: Evidence for classical EDS should not be presented as definitive isolated aortic disease validity.

EFEMP2.relevance: Fibulin-4 is needed for elastic fiber formation. Biallelic disease can cause cutis laxa with marked arterial tortuosity, stenoses, and aneurysms.
EFEMP2.consideration: Review systemic connective tissue features and establish biallelic status.

ELN.relevance: Elastin is a major component of arterial elastic fibers. Different variant mechanisms can cause obstructive arterial disease or autosomal dominant cutis laxa.
ELN.consideration: Distinguish haploinsufficiency-related stenosis from cutis-laxa mechanisms and associated vascular findings.
ELN.caution: Broad vascular-panel inclusion does not mean all ELN variants confer thoracic aneurysm risk.

FBN1.relevance: Fibrillin-1 forms extracellular microfibrils. Pathogenic variants can cause Marfan syndrome and related disorders with aortic, ocular, and skeletal involvement.
FBN1.consideration: Integrate aortic root imaging, ocular findings, systemic assessment, and the variant mechanism.

FBN2.relevance: Fibrillin-2 supports elastic microfibril development. Pathogenic variants typically cause congenital contractural arachnodactyly with contractures and skeletal features.
FBN2.consideration: Distinguish the contractural phenotype from Marfan syndrome; vascular interpretation should follow the specific diagnosis.
FBN2.caution: The evidence base for isolated HTAD is less established than for FBN1.

FLNA.relevance: Filamin-A connects actin to cellular signaling structures. Certain FLNA disorders combine neurodevelopmental, valvular, connective tissue, and aortic features.
FLNA.consideration: Ask about seizures and neurological imaging; variant mechanism and sex affect the syndrome.

LOX.relevance: Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen and elastin. Pathogenic loss-of-function variants can weaken the aortic extracellular matrix and cause heritable thoracic aortic disease.
LOX.consideration: Assess family aortic history and obtain specialist gene-specific vascular review.

MYH11.relevance: Smooth muscle myosin heavy chain supports vascular contraction. Pathogenic variants can cause familial aortic disease, sometimes accompanied by patent ductus arteriosus.
MYH11.consideration: Aortic disease plus a PDA in the family is a useful clue; variant mechanism needs review.

MYLK.relevance: Myosin light-chain kinase regulates smooth muscle contraction. Pathogenic variants can cause aortic dissection, sometimes without marked preceding dilation.
MYLK.consideration: Family dissection history and gene-specific specialist assessment are important; diameter alone may not capture risk.

NOTCH1.relevance: NOTCH1 signaling is important for cardiovascular development. Pathogenic variants can cause left-sided congenital heart disease, including bicuspid aortic valve.
NOTCH1.consideration: Interpret alongside valve anatomy and family history; assess aortic findings on their own merits.
NOTCH1.caution: Congenital valve disease validity differs from limited evidence for isolated HTAD.

PRKG1.relevance: Protein kinase G regulates smooth muscle relaxation. Selected activating variants can cause familial aortic disease and dissection.
PRKG1.consideration: Review the specific gain-of-function mechanism; do not apply known high-risk variant data to every rare change.

SKI.relevance: SKI regulates developmental signaling. Pathogenic variants cause Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome with craniosynostosis, skeletal features, and possible aortic involvement.
SKI.consideration: Look for the syndromic phenotype and seek connective tissue/genetics assessment.

SLC2A10.relevance: GLUT10-related disease affects connective tissue and arterial integrity. Biallelic variants can cause generalized arterial tortuosity with stenoses and aneurysms.
SLC2A10.consideration: Confirm biallelic status and review the wider arterial tree and systemic connective tissue phenotype.

SMAD2.relevance: SMAD2 transmits TGF-beta signals. Disease-associated variants can cause a connective tissue disorder with arterial aneurysm, tortuosity, and variable syndromic features.
SMAD2.consideration: Use the exact gene-disease pair and specialist vascular assessment; expression varies within families.

SMAD3.relevance: SMAD3 is a TGF-beta signaling mediator. Pathogenic variants can cause widespread arterial disease, often with early osteoarthritis.
SMAD3.consideration: Early joint degeneration alongside aortic or other arterial disease is a useful diagnostic clue.

SMAD4.relevance: SMAD4 integrates TGF-beta signaling. Certain variants cause juvenile polyposis with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, with aortic involvement reported in some affected individuals.
SMAD4.consideration: Review GI polyps, bleeding, telangiectasia, and AVMs; variant mechanism distinguishes other SMAD4 syndromes.
SMAD4.caution: This is syndrome-oriented coverage, not equivalent evidence for isolated HTAD.

TGFB2.relevance: TGF-beta-2 participates in extracellular matrix regulation and vascular development. Pathogenic variants can cause heritable aortic disease with variable connective tissue features.
TGFB2.consideration: Review aortic and extra-aortic arterial findings and the family phenotype.

TGFB3.relevance: TGF-beta-3 signaling supports vascular and connective tissue homeostasis. Disease-associated variants can produce heritable thoracic aortic disease with variable syndromic features.
TGFB3.consideration: The PDF places this addition in a second-priority extension; seek current gene-specific expert guidance.
TGFB3.caution: Outcome data and disease validity are less extensive than for core HTAD genes; the GeneReviews overview lists limited HTAD evidence.

TGFBR1.relevance: TGF-beta receptor type 1 participates in vascular developmental signaling. Pathogenic variants can cause Loeys-Dietz syndrome and heritable aortic disease.
TGFBR1.consideration: Assess extra-aortic arterial and systemic features; use specialist gene-specific surveillance and intervention guidance.

TGFBR2.relevance: TGF-beta receptor type 2 participates in extracellular matrix and vascular regulation. Pathogenic variants can cause aortic and more widespread arterial disease.
TGFBR2.consideration: Evaluate the syndromic phenotype, family history, and extra-aortic vasculature with an experienced team.

ACVRL1.relevance: ALK1 is an endothelial BMP/TGF-beta pathway receptor. Pathogenic variants cause hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and can be associated with pulmonary arterial hypertension.
ACVRL1.consideration: Distinguish true pulmonary vascular disease from high-output pulmonary hypertension related to HHT vascular malformations.

ATP13A3.relevance: ATP13A3 participates in polyamine transport and endothelial homeostasis. Pathogenic variants can cause PAH, with more severe early disease reported in biallelic individuals.
ATP13A3.consideration: Assess allele dosage and family history; incomplete penetrance affects counseling.

BMPR2.relevance: BMPR-II transmits BMP signals needed for pulmonary vascular homeostasis. Pathogenic variants are a major cause of heritable PAH with incomplete penetrance.
BMPR2.consideration: Offer specialist genetic counseling and family risk assessment after a confirmed pathogenic result.

CAV1.inheritance: AD; other inheritance in distinct disorders
CAV1.relevance: Caveolin-1 organizes endothelial membrane caveolae and signaling. Selected pathogenic variants are associated with pulmonary arterial hypertension.
CAV1.consideration: Interpret the allele and disease mechanism; lipodystrophy associations involve different clinical contexts.

EIF2AK4.relevance: GCN2 regulates the cellular stress response. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause heritable pulmonary veno-occlusive disease / pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis, which can resemble PAH.
EIF2AK4.consideration: PVOD/PCH needs expert distinction from PAH; pulmonary vasodilators can provoke pulmonary edema in this setting.

ENG.relevance: Endoglin is an endothelial BMP/TGF-beta co-receptor. Pathogenic variants cause HHT, with vascular malformations and pulmonary vascular complications.
ENG.consideration: Assess epistaxis, telangiectasia, and AVMs; distinguish high-output or shunt-related disease from PAH.

GDF2.relevance: BMP9 is a circulating ligand in pulmonary endothelial signaling. Disease-associated variants can impair vascular homeostasis and cause PAH or related vascular phenotypes.
GDF2.consideration: Review zygosity, functional effect, and the exact vascular presentation.

KCNK3.relevance: TASK-1 is a potassium channel that helps set pulmonary arterial smooth muscle membrane potential. Loss-of-function can promote pulmonary vascular disease.
KCNK3.consideration: Assess inheritance and variant function; the finding requires a pulmonary hypertension phenotype and expert classification.

KDR.relevance: VEGFR2 supports vascular endothelial signaling. Pathogenic loss-of-function variants have been associated with PAH, sometimes with reduced pulmonary diffusion capacity.
KDR.consideration: Review DLCO, pulmonary imaging, and phenotype-specific variant evidence.

SMAD9.relevance: SMAD9 transmits BMP pathway signals. Disease-associated variants can disrupt pulmonary vascular signaling and contribute to heritable PAH.
SMAD9.consideration: Consider reduced penetrance and use specialist counseling for family assessment.

SOX17.relevance: SOX17 is a transcription factor important for endothelial development. Pathogenic variants are associated with PAH, including pediatric disease with congenital heart defects.
SOX17.consideration: Review congenital cardiac anatomy and family history alongside the pulmonary vascular diagnosis.

TBX4.relevance: TBX4 directs limb and lung development. Pathogenic variants can cause PAH with skeletal clues or developmental lung abnormalities, particularly in childhood.
TBX4.consideration: Examine patellae, pelvis, and feet, and review lung development; skeletal findings may be subtle.

ABCG5.relevance: ABCG5 works with ABCG8 to export plant sterols. Biallelic loss-of-function causes sitosterolemia, an important familial hypercholesterolemia mimic.
ABCG5.consideration: Consider plasma plant sterols when xanthomas, premature ASCVD, or hematologic abnormalities suggest sitosterolemia.

ABCG8.relevance: ABCG8 pairs with ABCG5 to limit sterol absorption and promote excretion. Biallelic disease causes sitosterolemia with variable cholesterol elevation.
ABCG8.consideration: Plant sterol measurement can distinguish this disorder from conventional familial hypercholesterolemia.

APOB.relevance: Apolipoprotein B is the principal structural protein of LDL. Specific receptor-binding defects can cause familial hypercholesterolemia; other variant classes cause low LDL instead.
APOB.consideration: Interpret against the lipid profile and mechanism; not every APOB variant raises LDL cholesterol.

APOE.relevance: Apolipoprotein E mediates remnant lipoprotein clearance. Specific genotypes or variants can predispose to dysbetalipoproteinemia or rare dominant hypercholesterolemia.
APOE.consideration: Use genotype-specific interpretation with cholesterol, triglycerides, and secondary factors; this panel is not an Alzheimer risk assessment.
APOE.caution: Common APOE alleles have context-dependent effects and are not interchangeable with monogenic FH variants.

LDLR.relevance: The LDL receptor clears circulating LDL particles. Pathogenic variants cause familial hypercholesterolemia; biallelic disease is generally more severe.
LDLR.consideration: Confirm sequencing and deletion/duplication coverage; a confirmed result can support lipid specialist care and cascade assessment.

LDLRAP1.relevance: LDLRAP1 links the LDL receptor to the endocytic machinery. Biallelic loss-of-function causes severe hypercholesterolemia resembling familial hypercholesterolemia.
LDLRAP1.consideration: Establish biallelic status and phase; one pathogenic allele does not establish the recessive diagnosis.

LIPA.relevance: Lysosomal acid lipase releases cholesterol and fatty acids from stored lipids. Biallelic deficiency causes dyslipidemia and liver disease and can mimic familial hypercholesterolemia.
LIPA.consideration: Elevated liver enzymes or hepatomegaly are useful clues; confirm with appropriate enzyme and molecular studies.

PCSK9.relevance: PCSK9 regulates degradation of the LDL receptor. Gain-of-function variants reduce receptor availability and cause familial hypercholesterolemia; loss-of-function generally lowers LDL.
PCSK9.consideration: The direction of functional effect is essential. Distinguish a disease-causing gain-of-function allele from a protective loss-of-function allele.

LAMP2.relevance: LAMP2 supports lysosomal function. Loss-of-function causes Danon disease, an important HCM mimic that can present with marked hypertrophy, pre-excitation, skeletal myopathy, and learning difficulties.
LAMP2.consideration: Consider early severe LVH, elevated CK, and extracardiac findings. Both males and females can develop clinically significant cardiac disease.
